items.prose: Your right index finger rests on J and covers two columns, like its partner on the left.
items.question: Tap every key the right index finger presses.

feedback.correct: Y, U, H, J, N and M.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the J column and the column next to it, towards the middle.

byKey.one-col: You took only the J column. The index finger also covers the H column: Y, H, N.
byKey.with-b: You added B. B belongs to the left index finger, in the T G B column.

explain.text: The right index finger owns U J M and Y H N. B is not one of them, even though it looks central.

items.prose: Ana has `ana/Downloads/prices.csv`. She makes a **copy** of it in `ana/project/data`, and a **shortcut** to it on her Desktop. Then she deletes `ana/Downloads/prices.csv`.
items.question: What still opens the prices?

options.why: You treated the shortcut like the copy. A shortcut holds a path; that path now leads nowhere.
You swapped them. The copy is a second, separate file; the shortcut was only a pointer.

options.text: Neither: both depended on the original
options.why: A copy is a separate file with its own path. Deleting the original leaves it alone.

feedback.correct: The copy is a real file; the shortcut was a pointer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which of the two is an actual file.

explain.text: A copy is a second file with its own path, so it survives. The shortcut stored the old path, which is now empty. Deleting a shortcut never touches a file; deleting a file breaks its shortcuts.

items.prose: Ana's current folder is `src`. A script asks for `../data/prices.csv`.
items.question: Tap the file this path names.

feedback.correct: Up to `project`, then down into its `data`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start in `src`, take one step up for `..`, then follow `data`.

byKey.r-d-p: You jumped to the top. Without a leading `/` the path starts in `src`, and `..` goes up one step to `project`.

explain.text: `..` from `src` is `project`. Then `data/prices.csv` leads to the project's own file: `/home/ana/project/data/prices.csv`.

items.prose: Ana's current folder is `/home/ana/project/notes`. She wants the shared file `/data/prices.csv`, at the top of the machine.
items.question: Select all that apply: which paths name the shared file from here?

options.why: One step up reaches `project`, so this is the project's own file, not the shared one.
With no leading `/` this starts in `notes`, which has no `data` folder.

feedback.correct: The absolute path, and four steps up to `/`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Resolve each path from `notes`; count one folder per `..`.

byKey.up4: Count the steps: `notes` to `project`, to `ana`, to `home`, to `/`. Four `..` reach the top, where the shared `data` sits.

explain.text: The absolute path works from anywhere. The relative one needs four `..`: up to `project`, `ana`, `home`, then `/`. When a path climbs that far, the absolute path is clearer.

items.prose: Ana's script reads files as plain text, line by line.
items.question: Select all that apply: which files can it read as text?

options.why: A PNG stores pixels, not characters. A text reader sees symbol soup.
Excel packs its workbook into a compressed format. It is not plain text, even though it holds a table.

feedback.correct: CSV, Python and Markdown files are plain text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide from each extension how the inside is written.

explain.text: `.csv`, `.py` and `.md` are all written as plain characters. `.png` and `.xlsx` are not, so a text reader cannot use them.

items.prose: The terminal's `ls` compares names one character at a time, from the left.
items.question: Put these names in the order `ls` lists them, first at the top.

feedback.correct: Name order is date order here.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the year first, then the month, character by character.

explain.text: With YYYY-MM-DD the year decides first, then the two-digit month. So the character order matches the calendar.

items.prose: A colleague sends Ana a file called `.prices.csv`.
items.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: It is hidden, and its extension is `.csv`.
It is shown normally, and its extension is `.prices.csv`.
options.why: You took everything after the first dot. The extension starts at the last dot, and the leading dot hides the file.

options.text: It is hidden, and it has no extension.
options.why: The leading dot hides it, but the last dot still starts an extension: `.csv`.

options.text: It is hidden, so it cannot be a CSV.
options.why: Hiding changes only how the file is listed. The inside is still a plain-text table.

feedback.correct: The first dot hides it; the last dot starts the extension.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first character, then the last dot.

explain.text: A leading dot hides the file from the normal view. The extension is still what follows the last dot, `.csv`. Use `ls -a` to see it.
